title: The crack in the stone
body: Neachdan, a mason splitting rock for a well, breaks into a vein of hard coal that shows every colour in the break. That night a storm comes over the hills, and lightning strikes the broken vein, and it takes fire. He carries a burning coal home and lays the first hearth: it is the first fire of the Ròdaich. On it he tries the other coals he broke out, and all burn alike, with a low black flame; he is glad of the fire all the same.

title: Three wells claim the crack
body: Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the mason's well was theirs, and that the lightning fell there. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip; the other two have only the telling. Between the three no chronicler has ever judged.

title: The slab over the burnt vein
body: When the fire in the vein has burned itself out, the mason's people dig no further. They lay a flat stone over the broken vein, draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw off. In this all the tellings agree.

title: The high snowfields shrink
body: Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still. On the gravel terraces of its lower reach lie hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water rose to it.

title: The first hearths of the high valleys
body: Hearths are made at Achadh dhìreach, of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them. There is no coloured coal in them: those who sat there had none of it, or would not burn it.

title: The oak comes to the lowlands
body: The birch and pine of the cold years give way to oak and hazel, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. The grove that names the place stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.

title: The bare north-west
body: The oak never reaches the north-western horn of the island. The gales off the north-western sea keep it bare, low heather and blanket bog behind the shore without a tree, as it is still. No hearth of that age has been found there.

title: Eilean dhubh cut off
body: The rising sea floods the low neck of land that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island. The hearths of the neck lie drowned under the sand of the sound, and the deer of the island, cut off, grow smaller in the lifetimes after.

title: Hunters on Eilean mhin
body: Seal-hunters pitch camps on Eilean mhin, coming there by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Rodos crossed open water of set purpose. The camps are kept a season at a time and left.

title: Seals on the skerries
body: Hunters of the north shore go out in skin boats in the autumn gales to the skerries off Eilean fhada, where the grey seals haul out to pup, and take them there. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast bear the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. On Eilean fhada a hard year is counted by the boats the gales kept ashore.

title: The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal
body: Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.

title: The middens of Seann Dunn
body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin the great mound at Seann Dunn: limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes until it stands taller than a man. It is the first sure trace of them. No tool in it is shaped as any later Ròdach shaped tools.

title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen
body: At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the eldest mark on Rodos made again and again of purpose.

title: The Keeper in the grove
body: In the oak grove at Doire ghlas a figure of grey smoke comes to Diarmad of the Mason's line, who has asked why the coal of the vein has colours. It names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the kin's keeper, and tells him of the making of the world by Caoran, the Young God, and of the gift hidden in the coal. Asked how the colours may be opened, it gives a riddle: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. From Diarmad's line the telling of the making goes to every hearth.

title: The mole at Seann Skell
body: A mole of unmortared boulders is laid out into the Abhainn naomh from the bank at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats from the current. Its foot lies under water still at the lowest tides, and every quay wall built there since stands on it.

title: The steps of Seann Bhral
body: Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. Their treads are worn hollow in the middle. How many feet that took, none has reckoned.

title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg
body: The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes facing the mainland. Forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this time is found on the mainland.

title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll
body: At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a shelf of rock into a pool beside the Abhainn uaine, with a slot for a wattle gate. When the river falls the gate is dropped and the pool emptied by hand. The slot is sharp still.

title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr
body: A road of crushed shell is laid across the reed marsh at Seann Warr, on the western shore of Loch chrom, a little over a mile long and raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the eldest made road on the island that may still be walked.

title: The script appears at Seann Tarr
body: Rows of signs are cut into the cliff above Seann Tarr, in the script that is found afterwards on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais, and none has read it. No sign of it has a meaning that all accept.

title: The gold coal takes fire on the sea
body: Aodh of the Mason's line carries the seven coals of the vein down to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands, and throws them into the sea one by one. The coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the water and burns gold until the waves put it under; the other six sink. It is the first of the Seven Coals to be lit from its own spirit.

title: The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
body: Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn, to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Rodos made for a trade, and not for sleep or for the dead.

title: The slipways of Seann Bhrenn
body: Long ramps of flat stone are laid down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat. Of the hulls nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went.

title: The lake dwellings of Loch chrom
body: Platforms on oak piles are raised in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of those years, is not known.

title: The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn
body: A whale strands below the southern Seann Dunn, and its ribs are raised for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The ribs are set up again in new houses at least twice before they rot.

title: The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell
body: At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted there.

title: The tower at the north-western Seann Skell
body: At the least of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, a single round tower of dry stone is raised, hollow-walled, with a stair in the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is afterwards seen.

title: The huts of the northern Seann Toll
body: At Seann Toll on the north coast a cluster of stone huts is built in the lee of a dune. The dune afterwards buries them whole, and the sand keeps them.

title: The eastern Seann Bhral
body: At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.

title: The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn
body: At the second Seann Mhorn, on the southern coast, oyster, whelk and cockle shell is heaped over a whole headland, and there is little else. The oysters of its lowest layers are larger than any taken there since.

title: The twin landings of Seann Bhrenn
body: A second Seann Bhrenn, far to the north-east of the first, has the same long ramps into the water. Whether the two were of one people, or only the name was carried, is not known.

title: The snowflake coal takes fire in the air
body: Fearghas of the Mason's line climbs to the highest ground of the island, above where Muileann gheal now stands, and lets the six unlit coals fall from the top. The coal flecked with white stars takes fire as it falls and burns white in the air; the others strike the stones cold. The summit is called after the kindred Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point.

title: The cliff-house at Seann Tarr in the east
body: At the Seann Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a single long house is built into a cleft of the cliff, with the living rock for its back wall. The rock behind the hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.

title: The north-eastern Seann Vell
body: The Seann Vell on the Abhainn bheag, a short way above its mouth in the north-east, is a small place of four houses and a boat-shed. No Seann-Dhaoine dwelling on the main island is known further to the north-east.

title: The northern Seann Skell
body: At the Seann Skell below the later Ros gheal, on the north coast, the Seann-Dhaoine lay a second breakwater, shorter than the southern one and curved against the swell of the open sea. The two moles are built the same way, stone by stone.

title: The western Seann Vell
body: At the Seann Vell of the west coast the Seann-Dhaoine dig a line of storage pits into the dune, lined with clay and lidded with slabs. Some held fish bones still when they were opened.

title: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire raised
body: On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, the Seann-Dhaoine build the walled outpost afterwards called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate looks inland, away from the sea.

title: Làrach an Dùin raised
body: A greater work is raised on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut into the bedrock, and room within, as it was later reckoned, for four hundred people and their beasts. Whether the builders of the outpost built this also has never been settled.

title: The kerbed way between the forts
body: A kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, is laid through the ground near Àth fhionn toward both strongholds. It is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have made away from the shore.

title: Làrach an Teampaill raised
body: A stepped platform of fitted stone is built in the eastern hills, with an altar block on its top step. The altar is set square to the central mountains. Every later temple on Rodos faces some other way.

title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east
body: A shaft is sunk straight down through the rock at the eastern Toll-dubh, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp will show. No spoil lies beside it. Whatever was taken out was carried away, or nothing was.

title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the west
body: A second shaft of the same making is cut at the western Toll-dubh, far across the island from the first. Stones thrown into either are not heard to land.

title: The First Canoe
body: Among the coastal Tuathaich families a half-forgotten telling of a voyage is kept, long hushed: a steersman with a name, and a first crossing to an isle of the blessed. Their church tells it as the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The druids of the Old Faith call it idle belief.

title: The black coal warm in the ground
body: Brian of the Mason's line buries the five unlit coals deep in the ground beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach. When he digs them up on the next day the black coal, as black as a wet crow, is warm in his hand and smoulders as the air comes to it; the other four are as cold as the clay.

title: Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr
body: The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide. Who rowed them, and from where, is not known.

title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted
body: Old sailors tell of a vast creature dwelling in the waters off the north-western coast. No wreck has ever been brought up to prove them wrong.

title: The beacon on the Baile chrom headland
body: A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands, and its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, and never to bring them in.

title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh
body: Seven boats are lost from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss laid at the door of the Sea-Watcher by name; before this it was feared only in general.

title: The seal hunt moves south
body: The hunters of the north-west leave the open water and work the southern side of the headlands, out of its sight. The seal bones thin in the middens of the north-west and grow at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag.

title: Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills
body: Inscriptions are cut on rock faces all across the Doire uaine hills, more than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some lines are cut over and defaced with the same kind of tool that made them.

title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine
body: The inscriptions of the Doire uaine hills tell of something that walked without breathing, and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight.

title: The hill fires go under the ground
body: After the inscriptions the hearths of the Doire uaine hills are dug into pits and roofed with slabs. No open hearth shows in those hills for many lifetimes. The people stay, and hide their light.

title: The nine at the hill camp
body: Nine people die inside a hut at the camp where Muileann chiar was afterwards built, and lie where they fell beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound is found on any bone. The hut is never opened again, and none is buried from it.

title: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside
body: A forest is held sacred long before any order of the Old Faith claims it. The trees knew it first, the old telling says, and the people after.

title: No axe in the grove
body: The families at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar carry their fuel a half-day's walk sooner than cut a branch within it. The charcoal in their hearths is of every wood but that one.

title: The white stag of the grove
body: Three hunters see a white stag at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and none of them draws. This is the first telling of it. The stag returns in the tellings of every age after, and the druids of later ages name it the white stag of Flidais; in this age it has no god.

title: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed
body: A second forest, that seems older than the first, is never settled, never felled, and never walked from end to end.

title: The paths that stop at a line of stones
body: Tracks are worn toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three quarters, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Beyond the stones the ground is not worn.

title: The blood of the misstrike
body: Cormac of the Mason's line carries the four unlit coals to the grove at Doire ghlas, where the Keeper first spoke, and sets about breaking them there. His hammer misses and opens the back of his hand, and where the blood falls on the red-brown coal it takes fire. The kindred call it the coal of life.

title: The deer-drives of the eastern forest
body: Lines of stakes and brush are set to drive the red deer of the eastern woods into a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest.

title: The first dog graves
body: At Cnoc fhionn in the east dogs are buried beside people, each with a shell at its head. No beast was given a grave on Rodos before.

title: The geese of Eilean ghorm
body: The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm come into the tellings for the first time. They come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and none hunts them there.

title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine
body: At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their greatest landing is at Seann Skell, up the Abhainn naomh, where the mole already stands.

title: The warm springs used
body: Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh. The people buried near them have old breaks that knitted clean. Here the sick of Rodos are first brought for healing.

title: The gate of the outpost walled up
body: The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from within. Those who did it left by another way, or did not leave.

title: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned
body: The outpost is deserted. It lay in ruin before the first trusty chronicles, and it is older than any dwelling of the Ròdaich. Who built it none knows.

title: The fortress cistern fouled
body: The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. Its water had served four hundred people. No one draws from it again.

title: Làrach an Dùin abandoned
body: The fortress is deserted in like manner, and is as much a riddle as the outpost. Whether both had the same builders has never been settled.

title: The temple altar stripped
body: The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are sharp still. It has never been found, and what was cut on it, if anything, is not known.

title: The silver coal in the river
body: Eòghann of the Mason's line drinks from the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach and says, 'This water tastes different from the sea water.' He throws the three unlit coals into the stream, and the coal with the sheen of silver takes fire in the current and burns silver under the water. The coal of fire and the rainbow coal lie dark.

title: Làrach an Teampaill abandoned
body: The temple is deserted. It is older than any faith that has a name, and its altar looks to the central mountains and the vein beneath them, away from the sea.

title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore
body: The high places are left, and every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is made within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as those of Seann Dunn once did.

title: The ancient sea-way
body: The boats of the Seann-Dhaoine keep a lane along the south-east coast, from the river mouth below Seann Dunn round the cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg now stands to the bay of Ceann chaol. Flat landing-stones lie along it a day's rowing apart, some grooved still by hauled keels. The Ròdaich call it Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way, and the fishers of that coast keep to it yet.

title: The hill-folk of the vein
body: In the high valleys about the crack dwells a people other than the Seann-Dhaoine, who call themselves Clann nan Dè, the godkin. They bury their dead in the ground and not on islands, and they cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them, no telling knows; their own word, later, is that they were always there.

title: The first small burning
body: At Àth gharbh a sliver of the coloured coal is burnt to a bead in a peat fire by a household not of the Mason's line. It burns black-flamed like any other coal, and the hearthstone round it is stained through with colour. No older burning of the coal by other hands is known. It is a small thing: one sliver, one fire.

title: The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach
body: At Achadh dhìreach the hill-folk rub broken coal from the vein into the wool of the dead, and it takes streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. It is seldom done: one grave in some thirty.

title: A sliver in a Seann Bhral midden
body: A chip of the coloured coal, still staining the shell about it, is thrown on a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. By gift, by trade or by theft a piece of the vein came to the Seann-Dhaoine; which, is not known.

title: The Children of the Question
body: The households of the high valleys begin to call the Mason's line Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair, the Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal, for their long questioning of the two dark coals; the lists shorten it to Clann na Ceiste, the Children of the Question. The kindred take the name, and Clann a' Chlachair is heard less after.

title: Carragh Cnoc bheag raised
body: A standing stone is raised, on which four words are afterwards found carved: Bha teine sa chloich, "there was fire in the stone."

title: The older face of Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: On the upper face of the stone runs a line of the unread script. The four Ròdais words lie lower, cut with a narrower tool by another hand. When that second hand came is not known.

title: Colbh Cnoc chiar raised
body: A second stone is raised, bearing only two words: Cuimhnich an teine, "remember the fire." Who is bidden, and why, none has ever said.

title: A ring of fire-stones round the pillar
body: The ground about Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring and paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires the size of hearths are kept there again and again. Nothing else is left.

title: Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised
body: A third stone is raised, and on it the whole of the saying: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. Here, it may be, the belief was first spoken.

title: The fire in the fingers
body: Seathan of Clann na Ceiste, who has handled the coal of fire all his days to no end, snaps his fingers when a thought strikes him, and the coal-dust on his hand takes fire. He beats it out against his coat and is not burned. So the sixth coal is lit, by the fire that is in the hand itself.

title: The gatherings at the column
body: People come to the column at Cnoc ghorm in numbers. The post-holes of shelters for some hundreds lie about it, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there was said to a crowd.

title: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated
body: A burial-ground grows about a place that none remembers hallowing. Its oldest graves are older than the oldest names that can be read there.

title: The black chip in the child's grave
body: A child is buried at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach with a sliver of the coloured coal closed in one hand. The sliver stains still the cloth it is kept in. No other piece of the vein is found with the dead of this age.

title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
body: The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The first rows are straight. The later ones bend round older graves that no one will disturb.

title: The panther roads
body: The great cats of the island are first seen to keep their roads, crossing the mountains by fixed ways at fixed seasons. Why they do so no one has learned.

title: The crossing season kept
body: The hill-folk learn the panthers' seasons and keep off the high passes while the cats cross. The camps in the passes stand empty at the same point in every year.

title: Eleven lost on the panther road
body: A party of eleven from the southern shore goes up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season and does not return. Years afterwards their bones are found along the line the cats use still.

title: The rainbow coal lit by the Keeper
body: Ailean of Clann na Ceiste, having lit each of the six coals again by its own way, carries them burning to the grove at Doire ghlas with the last coal, which his kindred have tried for more than four hundred years. The Keeper comes to him there and lights the rainbow coal, and for the first time all seven burn together, each from its own spirit. It bids him stay with them until they are cold.

title: The vigil and the crowning
body: Ailean keeps watch by the seven fires for seven nights, fasting, a night for each coal. On the eighth night the coals are cold, and Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè about him. He names Ailean Rìgh Chlann nan Dè, king of the godkin, and puts into him the power that was in the coals. Of that power Ailean tells no one while he lives.

title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings
body: Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove, comes down to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and takes it, and brings the households of the valleys about it under his hand: the first kingdom of the godkin. How he won, none who stood against him could say. He throws up the hill's first ring of bank. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Ròdaich.

title: The bank of Dùn ìseal
body: The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.

title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill
body: Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.

title: Gormshuil nic Ailein
body: Gormshuil nic Ailein, second of the Stone Kings, is the first woman named in any list on Rodos. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.

title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones
body: Dòmhnall Clachach, third of the Stone Kings, sets marker stones along the valley below the hill to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.

title: The first named storm
body: A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.

title: The shell road broken
body: The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.

title: Fearchar Bacach
body: Fearchar Bacach, the lame king, rules at Dùn ìseal after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Rodos remembered for a hurt.

title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill
body: Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.

title: Strokes on the midden stones
body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.

title: The counting of the dead begins
body: The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Ròdaich to take up the custom.

title: The tally wall of Seann Warr
body: At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.

title: The count at Seann Tarr
body: The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.

title: The bad years in the counts
body: The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.

title: The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen
body: At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.

title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent
body: After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.

title: The old names kept
body: The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.

title: The old landings taken up
body: Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.

title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid
body: Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept.

title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm
body: Shallow clay basins are made behind a shingle bar at Baile ghorm, the first salt-works of the island. From this time their salt is found in the hill settlements.

title: Seonag of the Red Hill
body: Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill after her father. It is told that she counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household was gone.

title: The first pots at Doire shean
body: Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, are first made at Doire shean on the south-west coast. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore uses them.

title: The dug-out at Cidhe Beag
body: A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. No older boat on Rodos is known in its whole shape.

title: Iain Dubh killed
body: Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to raid the salt-pans as Mòrag Chruaidh had done, and is slain on the shingle at Baile ghorm. The list says only that he was brought home.

title: The wave at Cnoc chaol
body: The sea comes far inland over a village on the site of Cnoc chaol and leaves a sheet of sand a hand thick upon its hearths, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The village is not rebuilt on the same ground.

title: The ground opens at Cill ghlas
body: A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas, and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and build on neither side of it.

title: The fault-line kept clear
body: A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and for the rest of the age no house is built within a stone's throw of it. Part of the line remains.

title: The unlit hearth
body: In a single dwelling a hearth is laid and never lit. Peat keeps it by chance. It is the eldest sign that someone here chose not to burn what could easily have been burned.

title: Peat over the unlit hearth
body: The house of the unlit hearth lies under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the coloured coal beside it, none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.

title: The measured handful
body: In all the hill settlements a custom takes hold that no fire shall have more of the coloured coal than one cupped hand can hold. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. From it the Small-Burning Law of the next age is made.

title: The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach
body: A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the coloured coal at once, knowing nothing of what it holds. The house burns down with three within, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. Ever after the tellings use it to show why the handful is kept.

title: The watchers of the slab
body: Families near the crack take turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. What they watch for, none ever says.

title: Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace
body: Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the holder of the Red Hill at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both lists tell of the meeting, and in neither is the other named before it.

title: The ford gathering
body: The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are made. No meeting-place on the island has been used longer without a break.

title: Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill
body: Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. It is told that he walked the salt road himself every year, to be seen upon it.

title: Hill-folk on the western shore
body: Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of their kind on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fish from the shore and not from boats.

title: Amber from the Hawk bay
body: Amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and drilled for stringing; lumps of it lie in the middens below Seann Skell. A bead of the same amber lies in the oldest ground of the ford gathering, carried there the length of the island.

title: The first houses at Cathair dhomhain
body: Round houses are built by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts them among its holder's households.

title: Cattle in the north-west
body: Cattle come to Cnoc ghorm in the north-west, where the settlements had lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.

title: The long-house at Cathair gheal
body: A long-house forty paces long, with byre and hall under one roof, is built on the rise at Cathair gheal. It is the greatest building of the age in the north-west. Twice it burns, and twice it is rebuilt on the same footing.

title: A youth let down into Toll-dubh
body: A youth is let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He is drawn up alive and never tells what lay at the bottom. No one goes down again in this age.

title: A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills
body: A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. Their hut is found empty, the fire still burning. Thereafter the covered hearth is kept more strictly.

title: The lake dwellings burn
body: The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one builds on the lake again in this age.

title: Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan
body: Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a wick of moss are used at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Rodos that is not a hearth, and they give little smoke.

title: The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich
body: Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used again and again through the rest of the age.

title: The upright looms of Muileann leathan
body: At Muileann leathan in the north cloth is woven on standing frames, no longer twined by hand. The loom-weights of fired clay lie in rows in the houses, where they fell from the warp.

title: The first tide-count
body: Someone begins to mark the high-water line against a fixed rock. Why is not told; but the marks are cut at intervals more even than a fisherman's need would ask, as later scholars observe.

title: A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain
body: The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth, the marks cut at the same intervals as on the first rock. Someone carried the practice there, and the interval with it.

title: The lake is higher
body: The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper, and by the end of the age Loch chrom stands a hand higher on the rock than at the first cut. The keepers go on cutting.

title: The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh
body: A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Rodos. Its grey flakes are carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other.

title: The flint road
body: A track is worn by the flint-carriers from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Near Àth leathan their feet sink it a yard deep.

title: The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
body: A hawk is carved on a lintel over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird.

title: Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: At Tobar fhiadhaich wolves are buried whole and with care, laid on their sides as people are. No other beast is so buried in this age.

title: Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years
body: Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. No deed is told of her but that she held, and the list goes on after her.

title: The hunger at Baile chrom
body: Hunger comes to the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom. Its pots are left full of boiled bark and seaweed, and its grave-rows are doubled. No older hunger on Rodos is tied to a place.

title: The drought at Achadh shean
body: The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry so long that the field banks are forsaken and grown over. When people return they cut new fields on another line.

title: The naming of the wind directions
body: The eight winds are named, and every Ròdach sailor after uses the names. Their meaning is dark even to those who speak them, and they have never been changed.

title: The wind-stones of Ceann leathan
body: Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they put out.

title: The wind-names carried to the islands
body: The eight wind-names are used on Eilean fhada as on the main island. The markers on its high point bear eight cut notches, one facing each way.

title: Tormod Liath
body: Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, outlives three heirs, and is remembered as old. In his time Dùn ìseal is given its second bank, and its ground is doubled.

title: The Ròdaich name
body: In this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Ròdaich and the island Ròdos. The first use is not known; the eldest tellings take both names for granted. With the names goes the belief: they did not come; they were here.

title: The first forbidden marriage
body: A marriage between two lineages is forbidden, for a reason no surviving telling gives. Already the Ròdaich order themselves by blood, long before the coal gives them cause.

title: Lines recited at the ford
body: At the ford gathering households begin to recite their lines aloud before any marriage is made, seven names back on either side. These are the first genealogies of the common households; only the Line of the Mason is older. None survives whole.

title: The first seeking of another vein
body: Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, seeking coal like the vein's. They leave it unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench stays open, and what it would have found is not known.

title: The stone that would not break
body: A second opening for a new vein is made elsewhere on the island and fails wholly: common rock, and nothing beneath it. So it is first known that the vein under the mountain is alone of its kind.

title: The prospecting ends
body: No one tries a third opening in this age. The Ròdaich hold that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choice is not theirs to try.

title: The first shared meal law
body: A custom arises, unwritten, that any household with food to spare shall share it before the storm season. Later it is made law, and later ages lean on it more than they own.

title: Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal
body: At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storms is done in the open: every household brings its surplus within the bank, and it is divided by the count of mouths. The custom has no earlier place that is known.

title: A household turned out at Àth shean
body: A household at Àth shean hides its spare grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first punishment under the custom that is remembered.

title: Eilidh Ghlas
body: Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered, the first fostering in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.

title: Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling
body: Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes the son of Eilidh Ghlas into his house. For it he is named Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and the Red Hill list calls him so more often than by his own name.

title: Oighrig, first keeper by lot
body: The families who watch the slab agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot, and no longer to take turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman called Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, and she keeps the slab for the rest of her life.

title: The keepers' house
body: A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for the holder of the lot, its door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Rodos made only to be near the vein.

title: The stone cup
body: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, that the handful of coal may be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it outlasts the age is not known.

title: The stone cup copied
body: Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each tried against the first by filling it with water. Thereafter the hill settlements measure the coal with one measure.

title: The meeting of the cups
body: The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups. The hill settlements return to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be tried.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag takes coal
body: A keeper by lot, Gilleasbuig Beag, is found with a basket of broken coal from the vein in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab, row him out to Eilean chrom, and leave him there without a boat. He is the first known to be exiled for the vein.

title: The coal returned to the crack
body: The coal from Gilleasbuig Beag's house is neither burned nor kept. The keeper after him carries it back to the slab and lays it beneath, piece by piece. The tellings make much of it: the coal went home.

title: Calum Ciar asks for the lot
body: Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households at the slab refuse him. The list sets down the refusal, which is more than it sets down of most things.

title: The kings and the keepers
body: After the refusal of Calum Ciar the lot is still drawn at the slab. The Stone Kings rule the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein, and the line between the two holds for the rest of the age. It is not yet written anywhere.

title: A' Ghaoth Dhubh
body: A storm called A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept.

title: The sharing holds after the Black Wind
body: The settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter out of their shared surplus. None on that coast is known to die of hunger that season.

title: The beacon at Baile ìseal
body: A fire is built on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. It is lit to bring boats home in a storm, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.

title: The beacon at Muileann bheag
body: A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. Under the tower the ash goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.

title: The beacon at Àth dhearg
body: Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral, and less worn.

title: The beacon at Tobar dhearg
body: A fire is kept for the boats of the south coast on the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands. With Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg the coasts of the island are lit at five points.

title: The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell
body: Four watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell see a back as long as three boats rise and go under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher tied to a named place and a count of witnesses.

title: Wreckage in the western water
body: For a season planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up along the western shore below the waters where raiders are afterwards seen. No bodies come with them, and no settlement on that coast lacks a boat.

title: Anndra Breac says 'we came'
body: At the ford gathering Anndra Breac, a teller of the western coast, recites a telling in which the people came to Rodos over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down, and he is put out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept; only the memory that he told it.

title: The doctrine said at the column
body: After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. From this time it is said as a rule, and not only held as a belief.

title: The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock
body: The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low. Her pairs can be read still. The keepers after her go back to single marks.

title: A third tide-rock at Inis thais
body: Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the interval of Ros dhomhain. So three rocks are kept side by side. None tells why the interval is what it is.

title: Ros dhomhain grows
body: Ros dhomhain becomes the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish now from boats and not from the shore.

title: The Red Hill's harbour
body: The households of the Red Hill build a landing of laid stone at the river-mouth below the hill, where the harbour of Cathair dhearg is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.

title: Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill
body: Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the peace of the ford holds a generation more.

title: The foster-son returns
body: The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal, bringing the salt-songs of the west. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went.

title: The first songs kept
body: The salt-songs of the south and west are sung at the raking of the pans. They are the oldest songs on Rodos whose words are said to survive: a refrain of four lines, which no one can now wholly construe.

title: Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are made in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments of the island.

title: The panthers turn back
body: The great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills without crossing. The hill-folk read it for a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.

title: The cattle lost in the passes
body: Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night, and the herders come down with nothing.

title: The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain
body: At Baile dhomhain in the south the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at its end. It is the first mark made on the island for a season.

title: The wind-stone at Seann Chwen
body: One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Ròdach manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. In few places do the marks of the two peoples touch.

title: Boats named for the winds
body: The fishing households of Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is held unlucky, and the name of a boat that sinks is never given again.

title: The Tuam keepers
body: A family dwelling by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of thorn from the old graves. They bury none of their own there. They only keep it.

title: A grave at Tuam opened
body: Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into a grave older than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. They close it and move the row, and none opens that grave again.

title: Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Their small fires, each of a single night, lie all along the edge.

title: A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: A child of the settlement at Cnoc bheag goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The searchers stop at the stones, and the telling does not blame them.

title: The first house at Cnoc bheag
body: Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the edge of the forest. They take their timber from the far side of the river, and never from the unclaimed wood.

title: The spring at Muileann ruadh
body: Pilgrims come in numbers to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and a ring of shelters is built there. Here is set the eldest healing-tale of Rodos: a herder came lame and walked home.

title: The Hollow Man seen again
body: Two herders passing the Doire uaine hills after dark see a figure walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and so, the telling says, they lived.

title: The covered hearth spreads
body: The covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements about Muileann chiar. From this comes the later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.

title: Settlers at Caol mhòr
body: Ròdach households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.

title: Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west
body: Households from Cnoc ghorm settle again the ground at Baile chrom that the old hunger had emptied. They dig their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.

title: Muileann àrsaidh settled
body: Houses are built on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint comes from Cnoc àrsaidh, and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.

title: The salt road to the north-west
body: A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford gathering to the north-west. At Muileann àrsaidh the salt costs three times its price at the pans, and is paid for in flint and seal-skins.

title: Doire ghlas settled
body: Households settle under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.

title: The east settled at Dùn thais
body: The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first stronghold of the Ròdaich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.

title: Achadh chaol cleared
body: Fields are cleared at Achadh chaol in the east by fire and by picking stones. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields still.

title: Cuan ruadh rebuilt
body: Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement of the east coast to build its walls against the wind and not only the cold.

title: Cathair fhada on the south coast
body: Cathair fhada is founded on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It draws its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug, and never speaks of where the well came from.

title: Caol ruadh on the southern strait
body: Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the cod of the strait on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast to hold more fish than shell.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr in the north
body: Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain, round a spring that never freezes. At its height it has some eighty houses, a great place for the age.

title: Baile gharbh in the north-east
body: Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.

title: Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast
body: Settlers build at Baile fhiadhaich on the western coast, where boars run in the thickets. They hang boar tusks over their doors, and boar is their chief meat for the rest of the age.

title: Cuan shean settled
body: Ròdach households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, beside an old landing of unknown builders, and use the landing without mending it.

title: Dùn chrom raised
body: A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the midst of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.

title: Cathair mhòr below the old outpost
body: Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it is the nearest quarry.

title: Cnoc naomh
body: Households come to settle on a hill for its spring, and the hill is already called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill. Why, is not known.

title: Tobar dhearg on the southern cape
body: The keepers of the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the greatest place on the south coast.

title: Muileann naomh founded
body: Muileann naomh is founded near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses stand on stilts over a marsh, and are afterwards moved to firm ground.

title: Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore
body: The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.

title: Seann Skell of the south
body: Ròdach households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell and keep its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.

title: Achadh shean resettled
body: Households return to Achadh shean after the drought and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.

title: Inis mhin settled
body: A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.

title: Muileann chaol on its hill
body: Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. Where the library stands now there is a cattle-fold.

title: Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol
body: At Muileann chaol a cairn is raised for each head of a household at death, on the slope above the fold. By the end of the age some forty stand there.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east
body: Baile Mòr ruadh grows up near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The middens of Seann Dunn lie a morning's walk away, and the settlers do not dig into them.

title: The temple ruin avoided
body: The Ròdaich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill without stopping and take no stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.

title: Ceann leathan's contests
body: At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones ends with wrestling and the lifting of stones. The heaviest, a black boulder, lies on the point still, and few have raised it.

title: The ford gathering grows
body: The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is parted by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.

title: Stone axes from the north
body: Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west are carried all over the island. They are too fine for work; most are laid unused in graves or under house floors.

title: The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
body: The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade in nothing else, and the chips about it lie knee-deep. Before the age ends the quarry is forsaken, and the axes cease.

title: The moor takes the north
body: The oak falls back, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they stand yet. In the north this is remembered as the time the winters lengthened.

title: The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn
body: Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges, and in places lie beneath them.

title: A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol
body: A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing its fords with salt. Thereafter none crosses there in the wet season.

title: The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar
body: The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the midst of their settlement and cut on it a mark for every house lost: twenty-two.

title: A dry year on the eastern plain
body: The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs to drink. The shared surplus holds, and no deaths are counted.

title: A second wave on the south coast
body: The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than before. The new houses stand higher on the slope, and none is lost.

title: The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again
body: The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again, and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is broken in two places, and is laid again.

title: Cnoc bheag under the Carragh
body: Households settle on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that no door faces the stone.

title: The seal rocks of Inis bhàn
body: The households of Inis bhàn on the lower Abhainn ìseal take seals from the skerries off the river mouth by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.

title: Fields at Achadh mhòr
body: The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall that no one claims.

title: The harbour at Baile ghlas
body: The households of the Red Hill draw up their boats at Baile ghlas, along the lake shore from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the fishing harbour of the Red Hill.

title: Achadh naomh's spring-fields
body: Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and lead the water round it in channels. The spring is fenced before any house is.

title: Caol gharbh on the rough strait
body: Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. They lay paddles beside their dead.

title: Doire chiar
body: A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns at the fall of the year.

title: The river landing at Caol shean
body: Caol shean, on the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein, becomes the river landing of the hill households of the east. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up the river to it from the coast, and go on from it into the keepers' country.

title: Dùn dhearg raised
body: A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it says only that Dùn dhearg came not to the gatherings.

title: Dùn dhearg comes to the ford
body: In the time of Catrìona Mhòr the households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given ground of their own on the far bank.

title: Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
body: Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich in the south-eastern hills, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They take the calves and rear them, and their herds become the best in those hills.

title: Ceann àrsaidh
body: Households from the Red Hill settle the point at Ceann àrsaidh on the Abhainn fhionn. They find an old river landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.

title: Cnoc thais in the north-west
body: Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches carry water still.

title: Inis mhòr
body: Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east and live by the fish of its sheltered pools. They build their houses in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Rodos.

title: Baile gheal in the south-west
body: Baile gheal is founded on the south-western plain round a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from the shells of the old middens along the coast.

title: Àth bheag on the eastern coast
body: Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Their boats go out after the geese on the islands.

title: Catrìona Mhòr
body: Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal; hers is the last name in the spoken list. It is told that she knew every household of the hills by its line seven names back.

title: Seumas Òg of the Red Hill
body: Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill, and with him the spoken list of the Red Hill ends. In the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down.

title: The two lists recited together
body: At the ford gathering, in the time of Catrìona Mhòr, the list of the Stone Kings and the list of the Red Hill are recited one after the other from the first name to the last. It takes from dusk to dawn. For the first time both are heard whole.

title: Lots drawn for the slab
body: The lot for the keeper of the slab is drawn now among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keepers' house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place of pilgrimage.

title: The keepers number nine
body: The keepers of the slab are made nine, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and at no other time.

title: Coal in every hearth by the handful
body: Every household of the hills burns its handful of the coloured coal, measured in a copy of the stone cup, on one night in the dark of the year, the night later kept as Samhain. All burn at once by agreement, so that the low fires of the handful show on every hillside on the same night.

title: A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh
body: The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, where the two diggers were crushed, refuses its handful of coal for as long as any remembers. No household before it is known to have chosen not to burn at all.

title: Counting the households
body: The people of Catrìona Mhòr count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord of Dùn ìseal is said to have borne some nine hundred knots, the greatest count made on Rodos in this age.

title: The saying on the column recut
body: The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut in their old grooves by a hand from the hill of the Stone Kings. Some later readers hold that the recutting changed a letter; none can prove which.

title: The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed
body: Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they lay and build elsewhere.

title: Eilean ìseal given to the dead
body: The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, after the old manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or came to it of themselves, is not told.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag's island
body: Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was left, stays empty and unfished. His fire is seen on it for three nights, the tellings say, and then no more.

title: The keepers ask to be named
body: The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr to declare their charge before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her may draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She neither refuses nor agrees, and the matter is left to the next age.

title: The eve of the Binding
body: So ends the Ancient Age. The handful is kept everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the saying is spoken at every gathering. None of it is yet declared, and no oath is yet sworn over the vein. With that swearing the next age begins.
